title: Low Cholesterol Lifestyle
note: Demo snapshot of public ifanca.org content, for a training session only. Not an official IFANCA dataset. Content may be out of date. Check ifanca.org for current information.

blocks.text: High cholesterol is often referred to as the silent killer due to the lack of early warning signs. It has been linked to dietary restrictions, clogged arteries, strokes, and heart attacks, but it’s more complex than simply good or bad. Cholesterol’s correlation with lifestyle, especially exercise, is becoming better understood as a game-changer for improving cardiovascular health.

Cholesterol is a fatty substance found in every cell of our bodies and is essential for building cell membranes, synthesizing vitamins, and producing hormones. The body needs cholesterol to thrive and survive, and there are two main types.
Low-Density Lipoprotein (LDL): LDL contributes to plaque buildup in arteries and increases the risk of heart disease and stroke. LDL is commonly referred to as bad cholesterol.

High-Density Lipoprotein (HDL): HDL aids in the removal of LDL from the bloodstream by transporting it to the liver, where it is processed and excreted. HDL is commonly referred to as good cholesterol.

Triglycerides are the third important blood lipid, and along with LDL and HDL, make up a number known as total cholesterol. This is the number many of us check at annual exams. Triglycerides are defined in the Mayo Clinic’s, Triglycerides: Why do they matter? as “a type of fat found in your blood. When you eat, your body converts any calories it doesn’t need to use right away to triglycerides.” These are stored in your fat cells and released for energy if needed. Elevated levels of triglycerides increase a person’s risk of stroke and heart disease.

As we eat, the liver takes in proteins, carbohydrates, and fats, and produces cholesterol. Then it packages the cholesterol for transport throughout the body to help produce hormones, build cell membranes, aid in digestion, and waste excretion. In addition to being produced by the body, we ingest cholesterol every time we consume animal-based products. There is no recommended dietary intake of cholesterol, instead the guidance is to combine a reduced intake of saturated and trans fats with exercise and a healthy lifestyle.

Physical activity is a proven way to help regulate and reduce cholesterol levels. Exercise requires more energy than rest, so the body consumes more nutrients to match this energy need. Increasing physical activity leads to weight loss, and losing just five percent of total body weight can lead to a significant reduction in triglycerides. A 2015 study by J. D. Brown et al published by the National Library of Medicine showed, “Patients who lost five-ten percent of their starting weight showed significant reductions in total cholesterol, LDL cholesterol, and triglycerides.”

All physical activity is beneficial, but not all exercise influences cholesterol equally. Aerobic exercises such as walking, running, swimming, and cycling are most effective at reducing triglycerides and increasing HDL. This type of exercise increases your heart and breathing rate for extended periods. Anaerobic exercises such as lifting weights, High-intensity interval training (HIIT), and plyometrics also reduce cholesterol however not as efficiently as aerobic exercise. The best method is a combination of both.

The American Heart Association recommends, “at least 150 minutes per week of moderate-intensity aerobic activity or 75 minutes per week of vigorous aerobic activity, or a combination of both, preferably spread throughout the week.” Alongside this recommendation is one to add “muscle-strengthening activity on at least two days per week.”
Consistency is the determining factor when using exercise for cholesterol management.
“A brisk thirty-minute walk, five-days a week is enough to make a difference on your total cholesterol.”
Increasing the amount of exercise, or the aerobic intensity, will lead to a higher reduction in total cholesterol.

Along with its physiological effects on cholesterol, exercise is one of the best lifelong methods of weight-management. Excess weight and body fat, especially around the abdomen, is typically associated with higher LDL and triglycerides, and lower HDL. It doesn’t matter what you do, do it with passion and consistency.

Exercise is critically important to cholesterol management, but it works best when it’s part of a heart-healthy lifestyle. Since some of our cholesterol comes from the foods and drinks we consume, so diet is a central factor in managing cholesterol. A diet high in vegetables, fruits, grains, nuts, legumes, and healthy fats will provide nutrient rich energy sources while reducing saturated and trans fats. So, what are we supposed to eat?

Vegetables and fruits are high in vitamins, nutrients, fiber, and antioxidants. These support healthy digestion and make you feel full. Fatty fish, like salmon and mackerel, are high in Omega-3 Fatty Acids and are known to lower triglycerides. Unsaturated fats like those found in nuts, olive oil, and avocados provide a healthy source of fat and may improve total cholesterol. Limiting the amount of red meat, processed foods, and high-fat dairy will directly reduce the amount of cholesterol you consume.

While animal products contain cholesterol, they are a great source of high-quality protein, vitamins, mineral, and amino acids. When reducing intake in this category, keep in mind that a well-balanced diet can still consist of red meat, chicken, milk, yogurt, and even ice cream. Lifestyle changes are about sustainability with appropriate size portions.

After a physician clears you for exercise, it’s important to manage your expectations. Realistically, it takes three-to-six month of consistent effort to see noticeable changes in total cholesterol. Fortunately, you’ll notice physical changes much earlier which should motivate you to continue. After eight-to-twelve weeks of consistent exercise you’ll notice positive changes to your body shape and composition.

Some individuals may need medication alongside their lifestyle change, especially those with family history of heart disease or high cholesterol. Exercise is even more important in cases where medication is needed. Regular cholesterol screenings are one of the best tools available to manage your heart health. By choosing to consume a well-balanced diet, exercise regularly, and check your cholesterol, you’re playing an active role in physical well-being.
